name: Musicians in the Museum: Parvathy Baul
description:
Vasu Dixit, Composer & Musician in Conversation with Parvathy Baul
What does it mean to devote one’s life to a musical and spiritual tradition? And how does one find one’s own voice within a practice shaped by generations of practitioners?
In this edition of ‘Musicians in the Museum’, composer and musician Vasu Dixit will be in conversation with Parvathi Baul, one of the foremost practitioners of the Baul tradition. The conversation will trace Parvathi’s journey into Baul Sangeet, exploring the experiences, encounters and influences that have shaped her artistic and spiritual practice.
From her early encounters with the tradition to a life dedicated to its music, philosophy and performance, the conversation will also reflect on what it means to be a woman practising and carrying forward a tradition in which women practitioners have historically been fewer in number.
Through personal anecdotes and reflections on music, devotion and the transmission of cultural knowledge, the programme offers an opportunity to encounter the world of Baul music through the lived experience of one of its most distinctive contemporary voices.
About the Artist: Parvathy Baul

Parvathy Baul is a practitioner, performer and teacher of the Baul tradition from Bengal. An accomplished singer, instrumentalist, storyteller and painter, her practice emerges from the lineage of two eminent Baul masters, Sri Sanatan Das Thakur Baul and Sri Shashanko Goshai, under whom she studied closely. Rooted in a deep spiritual practice, her performances have taken her to over 40 countries and renowned international festivals and cultural institutions. A recipient of the 2019 Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, Parvathy is also committed to preserving and transmitting the Baul tradition through Sanatan Siddhashram, which she established in West Bengal, and her work in making traditional Baul learning accessible to women.
About the Interlocuto

Vasu Dixit is a Bengaluru-based musician, composer and filmmaker, best known as the lead vocalist of the folk-rock band Swarathma, which he formed in 2002. A graduate of the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad, Vasu brings together his interests in music, visual arts and storytelling in his creative practice. In 2017, he founded the Vasu Dixit Collective, an ensemble that explores electronic folk and folk-rock, drawing inspiration from Kannada and Hindi poetry and the works of saint poets such as Purandara Dasa, Basavanna and Kabir. His work reflects an ongoing exploration of musical traditions through contemporary expression.
About the Series: Musicians in the Museum
Musicians in the Museum is a series of artist conversations at the Indian Music Experience Museum that offers audiences an opportunity to understand the people and experiences behind the music. Through conversations with musicians from different genres and generations, the series explores their personal, professional and artistic journeys – from their early influences and formative experiences to their creative processes, challenges and evolving practices.
Previous editions have featured artists including Indian Ocean, Sumangala Damodaran and Dr Jayanthi Kumaresh. The series creates a space for audiences to engage with musicians beyond the stage and gain a deeper understanding of the stories, ideas and influences that shape their work.

name: Guru Nanak: The Mystic, the Poet
description:
A musico-literary exploration of Baba Nanak’s writings by Radhika Sood Nayak
Five centuries ago, Guru Nanak travelled across regions and faiths, sharing a message of oneness: Ik Onkar (ੴ), the belief that there is one eternal truth present in all creation. His teachings emphasised that all people are equal, love is central to a meaningful life, and honest work and good deeds are forms of devotion.
This Gurpurab, join Sufi vocalist and composer Radhika Sood Nayak for an evening of Shabads (hymns) from the Guru Granth Sahib. The programme will feature the Baanis of Guru Nanak, along with compositions by other Sikh Bhagats – saints and poets whose teachings continue to inspire generations.
Among them are Bhagat Kabir, the weaver-poet who spoke against ritual and social divisions; Bhagat Namdev, the devotional poet from Maharashtra; and Bhagat Ravidas, who imagined Begumpura – a city free from sorrow and inequality.
Their compositions emerged from the Bhakti movement, a significant socio-spiritual movement that challenged social hierarchies and emphasised devotion, equality and love. Their hymns continue to be an integral part of the Guru Granth Sahib, bringing together voices and traditions across communities.
Be part of an evening where music brings people together, transcending the divisions of caste, class and religion, and reminding us of the shared humanity at the heart of every faith.
 About the Artist: Radhika Sood Nayak

Radhika Sood Nayak is a vocalist, composer and narrator, rooted in Hindustani classical music. Her love for Sufi Kalaam was kindled by the poetry of 17th-century mystic Bulleh Shah.
Her journey began with the Mumbai Kabir Festival and she has since performed at Kabir yatras in Rajasthan and Malwa. Inspired by the poetry of Shah Hussain, she has composed new music and worked with artists from Lahore and Kutch to create music videos. Her renditions carry a quiet resolve to dissolve rigid identities and man-made borders.
Radhika holds an MBA from XLRI Jamshedpur and has worked in the corporate world before choosing to pursue music full time. Today she curates poetry-led musical performances, with her own narration in English, to take Panjabi poetry beyond borders.

name: Musicians in the Museum: Tarun Balani
description:
Conversations and a Vinyl Listening Session on cultural memory, migration & the making of music
How do cultural legacies endure through music as people, traditions and contexts move across borders?
In this edition of Musicians in the Museum, composer and drummer Tarun Balani reflects on these questions through his album Kadahin Milandaasin ڪڏهن ملنداسين (Sindhi for “When will we meet?”). A deeply personal work, the album draws on the life and legacy of his late grandfather, K.S. Balani, a celebrated Sindhi post-modern writer and painter. Through music, Tarun explores his relationship with Sindhi identity, ancestral memory and the experience of migration.
The programme will begin with a conversation facilitated by IME’s Programmes Manager Sarvar Kahlon  on Tarun’s personal and artistic journey, his creative process and the influences that have shaped his work. This will be followed by a guided listening session, featuring selections from Kadahin Milandaasin and other works from his repertoire, alongside music and sounds that have informed his practice.
Through conversation and listening, audiences will gain insight into how personal histories and cultural inheritances can find expression in contemporary music.
 About the Artist: Tarun Balani

Tarun Balani is a composer, drummer, artist and educator whose work brings together improvisation, composition, performance and technology. His music moves across contemporary jazz and electronic sound, often exploring themes of identity, migration, memory and the environment.
His recent albums include the critically acclaimed Kadahin Milandaasin and Where the Ice Meets the Water. His sound installation Listening Room reflects deeply personal experiences of climate anxiety and ecological grief, while also emphasizing the possibility of hope in a changing world. Through his recordings and live performances, Balani creates immersive musical experiences that draw on personal narratives, cultural influences and contemporary sound. 
About the Album: Kadahin Milandaasin ڪڏهن ملنداسين
Kadahin Milandaasin, meaning “When Will We Meet Again?”, is an album inspired by Tarun Balani’s late grandfather, K.S. Balani, a prominent Sindhi writer and painter. Drawing on family history, Sindhi culture and the experience of migration, the album explores how music can hold memories of people, places and traditions across generations.
Described by The Hindu as a “sonic love letter to Sindh”, Kadahin Milandaasin brings together musical influences rooted in Sindhi culture and folk traditions with contemporary composition and sound. The work offers a way to engage with a cultural history shaped by displacement, memory and the connections people maintain with the places they come from.
The work brings together contemporary jazz, ambient electronic music and sonic storytelling to create a personal reflection on identity, belonging and cultural inheritance. It has received international recognition, with features on NPR Music, JazzTimes and Bandcamp’s Best of Jazz 2025.
About the Series: Musicians in the Museum
Musicians in the Museum is a series of artist conversations at the Indian Music Experience Museum that offers audiences an opportunity to understand the people and experiences behind the music. Through conversations with musicians from different genres and generations, the series explores their personal, professional and artistic journeys – from their early influences and formative experiences to their creative processes, challenges and evolving practices.
Previous editions have featured artists including Indian Ocean, Sumangala Damodaran, Divyam Sodhi and Khwaab. The series creates a space for audiences to engage with musicians beyond the stage and gain a deeper understanding of the stories, ideas and influences that shape their work.
